questions.question: Which of the following Constitutional provisions can be amended by an ordinary Act of Parliament (simple majority), rather than through the special procedure under Article 368?

options.text: Article 2 (Parliament may by law admit new states)

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 2**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 2** of the Constitution of India provides **Parliament the power to admit new states into the Union of India** or establish new states.
 
• This article grants Parliament the authority to enact laws for the creation or admission of states through a **simple majority**, not requiring the special amendment process under **Article 368**.
 
• The provision under Article 2 is utilized when India integrates new territories or regions. For example, **Sikkim** was admitted as a state of India in **1975** under this article. *Hence, Article 2 can be amended by an ordinary Act of Parliament. Statement 1 is correct.*
 
• **Article 356** and **Article 368** require constitutional processes and cannot be amended by a simple majority. These provisions are subject to stricter conditions. *Hence, Article 356 and Article 368 cannot be amended by an ordinary Act of Parliament. Statement 2 and 3 are incorrect.*
 
• **Article 14**, which guarantees equality before the law, is a fundamental right enshrined in Part III of the Constitution. It cannot be amended by a simple Act of Parliament as it forms part of the basic structure of the Constitution. *Statement 4 is also incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 2 of the Constitution:**

 
 
• Article 2 grants Parliament the authority to admit new states or establish new states within the Union of India.
 
• It is a procedural article allowing the expansion of India's territorial boundaries through legislative action.
 
• Examples include the integration of **Sikkim** and creation of new states such as **Telangana** through reorganization.
 
 
 
• **Article 356:**
 
 
• This article empowers the President to impose **President’s Rule** in a state under certain circumstances.
 
• It requires specific legal and constitutional grounds, such as the breakdown of constitutional machinery in the state.
 
• It cannot be amended through a simple majority, as it forms a critical aspect of the federal structure.
 
 
 
• **Article 368:**
 
 
• Article 368 provides the procedure for amending the Constitution.
 
• It outlines a **special procedure** requiring a two-thirds majority in both Houses of Parliament and ratification by at least half of the state legislatures.
 
• Hence, amendments to fundamental provisions cannot be done via a simple majority.
 
 
 
• **Article 14:**
 
 
• Article 14 guarantees **equality before law** and equal protection of the laws to all individuals within the territory of India.
 
• It is a fundamental right forming part of the **basic structure of the Constitution**.
 
• Any amendment or change to this article requires the special procedure outlined in Article 368.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Provisions for Constitutional Amendments:**

 
 
• Constitutional provisions are categorized into two types for amendments: those amendable by a **simple majority** and those requiring the **special procedure** under Article 368.
 
• Provisions related to the organization of states, such as Articles 2 and 3, can be amended via a simple majority.
 
• Fundamental rights and structural provisions, such as Articles 14, 368, and others, require a special procedure for amendment.
 
• The basic structure doctrine, established in the **Keshavananda Bharati case (1973)**, ensures that certain provisions cannot be altered.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Reorganization:**
 
 
• Reorganization of states has been carried out under Articles 2 and 3, such as the formation of **Chhattisgarh** (2000), **Uttarakhand** (2000), and **Telangana** (2014).
 
• Such reorganizations are based on socio-political considerations, linguistic factors, or administrative needs.

questions.question: Which shortcut key opens System Settings quickly in Windows 10/11?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Windows + I**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Windows + I** is the shortcut key used to quickly open the **System Settings** in **Windows 10 and Windows 11**. It allows users to access various system configurations and options in one centralized location.
 
• The **System Settings** menu in Windows includes options like **Display settings, Network settings, Personalization, Updates, and Security**, among others.
 
• Using **Windows + I** is a faster alternative to manually navigating through the Start menu to find the settings application.
 
• This shortcut is highly efficient for users who frequently need to modify system configurations or check for updates.
 
• Unlike the other options provided, **Windows + I** is specifically designed for opening the Settings menu, making it the correct and most relevant choice.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Alt + F4:**

 
 
• This shortcut is used to **close the currently active window** or application. If no windows are open, pressing Alt + F4 will bring up the shutdown menu in Windows.
 
• It is not related to accessing the System Settings.
 
 
 
• **Ctrl + Alt + Del:**
 
 
• This combination brings up a menu that includes options like **Task Manager, Lock, Sign Out, and Change Password**.
 
• It is primarily used for security and system management purposes, not for accessing System Settings.
 
 
 
• **Windows + D:**
 
 
• Pressing Windows + D minimizes all open windows and shows the desktop.
 
• This shortcut is helpful for quickly accessing the desktop but does not open the System Settings.
 
 
 
• **Windows + I:**
 
 
• This shortcut is specifically designed to open the **Settings** menu in Windows, allowing users to configure and personalize their system.
 
• It is a universally recognized shortcut across both **Windows 10 and Windows 11**.
 
 
 
• **System Settings in Windows:**
 
 
• The Settings app is the central hub for managing system preferences, including **network settings, display options, user accounts, and security updates**.
 
• It was introduced in **Windows 8** as a replacement for the traditional Control Panel and has become more comprehensive in Windows 10 and 11.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Settings app** in Windows is distinct from the traditional **Control Panel**. While the Control Panel is still available, Microsoft is gradually transitioning most settings to the new interface.
 
• **Windows 11** introduced a redesigned Settings app with a more modern and user-friendly interface compared to its predecessor.
 
• Shortcut keys like **Windows + I** are part of Microsoft's effort to enhance productivity by providing quick access to frequently used features.
 
• Knowing these shortcuts can significantly streamline system navigation and reduce the time spent searching for specific options.

questions.question: Through which of the following states do the Western Ghats pass?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Tamil Nadu**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Western Ghats** is a mountain range that runs parallel to the western coast of the Indian peninsula, covering a total of six states in India: **Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu**.
 
• **Tamil Nadu** is one of the key states where the **Western Ghats** extend. The range in Tamil Nadu is known for its rich biodiversity and is home to various hill stations like **Ooty (Nilgiris)**, **Kodaikanal**, and **Coimbatore hills**.
 
• The **Western Ghats** in Tamil Nadu include the **Nilgiri Hills, Anamalai Hills**, and **Cardamom Hills**, which are significant for their ecological and economic importance.
 
• The range has been designated as a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** due to its exceptional biodiversity and is considered one of the **eight hottest hotspots of biological diversity** in the world.
 
• The states mentioned in the other options, such as **Punjab, Bihar, and Uttar Pradesh**, are located in the northern and eastern parts of India and are not traversed by the **Western Ghats**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Geographical Coverage of the Western Ghats:**

 
 
• The **Western Ghats** stretch across six states: Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu, covering a total length of approximately **1,600 km**.
 
• It forms the **watershed** for the **Peninsular Rivers**, including the Godavari, Krishna, and Kaveri, which are crucial for irrigation and drinking water.
 
 
 
• **Ecological Significance:**
 
 
• The Western Ghats is home to a large number of **endemic species** of flora and fauna, including the **Nilgiri Tahr** and the **Lion-tailed Macaque**.
 
• The range plays a critical role in influencing the **monsoon weather patterns** in the region and acts as a barrier to the southwest monsoon winds.
 
 
 
• **UNESCO World Heritage Site:**
 
 
• The Western Ghats was inscribed as a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** in **2012** for its exceptional natural beauty and unique ecosystem.
 
• It is recognized as one of the **eight hottest hotspots of biological diversity** in the world.
 
 
 
• **Hill Stations and Tourism:**
 
 
• The Western Ghats in Tamil Nadu is a significant tourist attraction due to the presence of popular hill stations such as **Ooty, Kodaikanal**, and **Valparai**.
 
• These hill stations are known for their **pleasant climate, tea plantations, and scenic beauty**.
 
 
 
• **Other States in the Question:**
 
 
• **Punjab:** Located in northern India, dominated by plains and does not feature the Western Ghats.
 
• **Bihar:** Situated in the eastern part of India, characterized by the Gangetic plains, and not traversed by the Western Ghats.
 
• **Uttar Pradesh:** A northern state predominantly covered by the Indo-Gangetic plains and not connected to the Western Ghats.

questions.question: Which of the following agencies collaborated on India’s first Quantum Key Distribution over a Multi-Core Fibre in 2025?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**C-DOT & Sterlite Technologies Ltd.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **C-DOT (Centre for Development of Telematics)** and **Sterlite Technologies Ltd.** collaborated to achieve India’s first **Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) over a Multi-Core Fibre**. This significant milestone in secure communication was achieved in **2025**.
 
• **Quantum Key Distribution** (QKD) is a cutting-edge technique that leverages the principles of quantum mechanics to ensure secure data transmission. It is a key enabler for secure communication in sectors such as defense, finance, and governance.
 
• QKD over a **Multi-Core Fibre (MCF)** is an innovative advancement that uses multiple cores within a single optical fibre to enhance the efficiency and security of quantum communication. This technology reduces latency and increases data transmission capacity.
 
• **C-DOT**, a premier R&D organization under the Ministry of Communications, has been pivotal in advancing India’s telecom technologies, including secure communication systems.
 
• **Sterlite Technologies Ltd.** is an Indian multinational company specializing in optical fibre and network solutions, playing a significant role in developing advanced telecom infrastructure and innovations in quantum communication.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Quantum Key Distribution (QKD):**

 
 
• QKD is based on the principles of quantum mechanics, particularly the **Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle** and **quantum entanglement**, ensuring that any eavesdropping attempt disrupts the data, making it detectable.
 
• It provides absolute security in data exchange, unlike traditional encryption methods that depend on computational difficulty.
 
• QKD applications include secure communication in **banking, defense, critical infrastructure, and governmental data**.
 
 
 
• **Multi-Core Fibre (MCF):**
 
 
• MCF technology uses multiple cores within a single optical fibre, enabling simultaneous data transmission across multiple pathways, increasing bandwidth and reducing latency.
 
• This technology is especially beneficial for **quantum communication systems**, which require high-speed and secure data transfer.
 
 
 
• **C-DOT (Centre for Development of Telematics):**
 
 
• C-DOT was established in **1984** as an autonomous telecom R&D center by the **Government of India**.
 
• The organization has been instrumental in developing indigenous telecom technologies and contributing to India’s **secure communication systems**.
 
 
 
• **Sterlite Technologies Ltd:**
 
 
• Sterlite Technologies Ltd. is a global leader in optical fibre and network solutions headquartered in **Pune, India**.
 
• The company has been actively involved in **5G infrastructure**, quantum communication, and digital transformation projects worldwide.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Global advancements in Quantum Communication:**

 
 
• Countries like **China** and **USA** have made significant progress in quantum communication, deploying QKD networks for secure inter-city communications.
 
• **China** launched the **Micius satellite** in 2016, the world’s first quantum communication satellite.
 
 
 
• **India’s Quantum Communication Initiatives:**
 
 
• The Government of India has earmarked **Rs. 8000 crore** for the National Quantum Mission to foster research and development in quantum technologies, including QKD.
 
• Collaborations between organizations like **C-DOT**, **ISRO**, and other research institutions are strengthening India’s position in quantum technology.

questions.question: The famous slogan "Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it " was given by _______.
questions.solution:

__
 
• The famous slogan "**Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it**" was given by **Bal Gangadhar Tilak**, a prominent leader in the Indian freedom struggle.
 
• This slogan became a rallying cry for the Indian independence movement and inspired millions of Indians to fight against British colonial rule.
 
• Tilak, often referred to as the "**Father of Indian Unrest**," was one of the first leaders to demand full independence for India.
 
• The slogan was used by Tilak in the context of his speeches and writings, particularly during the **Home Rule Movement** of 1916-1918, which aimed at achieving self-governance for India within the British Empire.
 
• Tilak's emphasis on Swaraj (self-rule) was instrumental in uniting people across the country against the British colonial government.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• Tilak was born on **23 July 1856** in Ratnagiri, Maharashtra, and is considered one of the most influential leaders of the Indian independence movement.
 
• He was a scholar, nationalist, and social reformer who advocated for Swaraj as a fundamental right of Indians.
 
• Tilak was also a prolific writer and edited newspapers such as **Kesari** (Marathi) and **The Mahratta** (English), which became platforms for expressing nationalist sentiments.
 
 
 
• **Home Rule Movement:**
 
 
• Started in 1916, the **Home Rule Movement** was led by Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Annie Besant to demand self-governance for India.
 
• Tilak’s leadership and his slogan energized the masses, making the movement a significant step towards India's independence.
 
 
 
• **Other Contributions of Tilak:**
 
 
• Tilak popularized the celebration of **Ganesh Chaturthi** and **Shivaji Jayanti** to promote unity among Indians.
 
• He authored books like "**Gita Rahasya**," which reflected his interpretation of the Bhagavad Gita as a call for action.

• **Mahatma Gandhi:** Known for his philosophy of non-violence and movements like Civil Disobedience and Quit India.
 
• **Subhas Chandra Bose:** Advocated armed struggle for independence and founded the Indian National Army (INA).
 
• **Dadabhai Naoroji:** Known as the "Grand Old Man of India," he highlighted economic exploitation under British rule through the **Drain Theory**.

questions.question: In April 2025, DOT announced funding of two specialised national testbeds for 6G R&D. One focuses on THz communication; which domain does the other explore?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Advanced optical communication**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In **April 2025**, the Department of Telecommunications (**DoT**) announced funding for two specialized **national testbeds** focused on **6G Research and Development (R&D)**.
 
• One of these testbeds is dedicated to **THz (terahertz) communication**, which is a crucial technology for ultra-high-speed data transmission and forms a core aspect of 6G development.
 
• The second testbed focuses on **Advanced optical communication**, a vital area for modern telecommunication systems, enhancing data transmission capabilities over long distances with minimal loss. *Hence, this is the correct answer.*
 
• **Advanced optical communication** involves the use of light for transmitting data through optical fibers, which is essential for achieving the ultra-low latency and high bandwidth requirements of 6G technology.
 
• The government is investing in such testbeds to ensure India remains competitive in next-generation telecommunications technology and to support academic and industrial research in these fields.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Advanced optical communication:**

 
 
• This technology uses **optical fibers** to transmit data at high speeds by converting electrical signals into light signals.
 
• It is characterized by **low latency, high bandwidth, and high data integrity**, making it essential for applications like 6G, autonomous vehicles, and IoT (Internet of Things).
 
• It supports key technologies like **Wavelength Division Multiplexing (WDM)**, which enhances data transmission by using multiple wavelengths of light.
 
• Research in advanced optical communication is paving the way for innovations like **quantum communication** and ultra-secure networks.
 
 
 
• **THz communication:**
 
 
• Terahertz (THz) communication operates in the **0.1–10 THz frequency range** and is a promising technology for ultra-high-speed wireless communication.
 
• It enables data rates of several terabits per second, which is a necessity for 6G networks and beyond.
 
• THz communication is expected to play a role in applications like **holographic communication, real-time AI processing, and immersive virtual reality (VR).**
 
 
 
• **Visible-light communication (VLC):**
 
 
• VLC uses visible light as a medium for wireless communication, often through LEDs.
 
• It is suitable for environments where **radio frequency (RF)** communication faces interference, such as in hospitals or aircraft cabins.
 
• While VLC has its advantages, it is not the focus of the testbed discussed in the question.
 
 
 
• **Quantum key distribution (QKD):**
 
 
• QKD is a **secure communication method** that uses the principles of quantum mechanics to encrypt and transmit data.
 
• It is considered to be unbreakable and is being actively researched for applications in **cybersecurity.**
 
• However, QKD is not the focus of the 6G testbed mentioned in the context of the question.
 
 
 
• **Satellite backhaul:**
 
 
• Satellite backhaul involves using satellites to connect remote areas to the core telecommunication network, providing **internet and cellular services**.
 
• It is especially useful for rural and geographically challenging locations but is not directly related to the testbed for advanced optical communication.

questions.question: Proteins are mainly responsible for which of the following?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Growth and repair of tissues**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Proteins** are essential macromolecules required for the **growth, repair, and maintenance of body tissues**. They play a crucial role in cell regeneration and healing wounds.
 
• Proteins are made up of **amino acids**, which are the building blocks necessary for the formation of muscles, skin, and internal organs.
 
• Unlike carbohydrates, proteins are primarily responsible for **structural and functional roles** in the body rather than being a quick energy source.
 
• Proteins also contribute to the production of **enzymes, hormones, and antibodies**, all of which are vital for maintaining body functions and immunity.
 
• In the absence of adequate protein intake, individuals may suffer from conditions like **muscle wasting**, weakened immune response, and delayed wound healing.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Functions of Proteins:**

 
 
• **Structural Function:** Proteins like collagen and keratin provide strength and support to tissues such as skin, hair, and nails.
 
• **Enzymatic Function:** Enzymes are proteins that catalyze biochemical reactions in the body, aiding in digestion, metabolism, and other vital processes.
 
• **Transport Function:** Proteins such as hemoglobin transport oxygen in the blood, while others assist in moving nutrients across cell membranes.
 
• **Immune Function:** Antibodies, composed of proteins, are crucial for fighting infections and ensuring immunity.
 
• **Hormonal Function:** Some hormones like insulin are protein-based and regulate various body functions, including blood sugar levels.
 
 
 
• **Sources of Proteins:**
 
 
• **Animal Sources:** Eggs, milk, meat, fish, and poultry are rich in high-quality proteins containing all essential amino acids.
 
• **Plant Sources:** Legumes, beans, nuts, seeds, and soy products provide protein for vegetarians and vegans.
 
• **Dairy Products:** Cheese, yogurt, and whey are excellent sources of proteins, especially for muscle repair.
 
 
 
• **Protein Deficiency:**
 
 
• Protein deficiency can lead to conditions such as **kwashiorkor**, characterized by swelling, fatigue, and poor growth.
 
• Individuals with inadequate protein intake may experience **weakened immune systems** and increased susceptibility to infections.
 
 
 
• **Quick Energy Sources:**
 
 
• **Carbohydrates:** These are the primary source of quick energy for the body, stored as glycogen and metabolized for immediate energy.
 
• Proteins are not typically used as a primary energy source unless the body is in a state of starvation or prolonged physical exertion.
 
 
 
• **Improving Digestion:**
 
 
• Proteins such as digestive enzymes (e.g., pepsin, trypsin) play a role in breaking down food into absorbable nutrients.
 
• However, proteins themselves are not directly responsible for enhancing digestion as a primary function.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Daily Protein Requirements:**

 
 
• The recommended daily protein intake varies based on **age, gender, and physical activity**. For an average adult, it is approximately **0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight**.
 
• Athletes and bodybuilders may require higher amounts to support muscle growth and repair.
 
 
 
• **Protein Quality:**
 
 
• Proteins are classified based on their amino acid content. **Complete proteins** (e.g., from animal sources) contain all essential amino acids.
 
• **Incomplete proteins** (e.g., from plant sources) may lack one or more essential amino acids but can be complemented by combining different food sources.
 
 
 
• **Proteins vs. Other Nutrients:**
 
 
• **Carbohydrates:** Primarily provide energy through glucose metabolism.
 
• **Fats:** Serve as long-term energy storage and support cell structure and hormone production.
 
• **Proteins:** Focus on structural, enzymatic, and functional roles rather than immediate energy provision.

questions.question: Why is canal irrigation more suitable in the northern plains of India?

__
 
• The **northern plains of India** are characterized by extensive flat lands, making them ideal for the construction of canal networks. The flat terrain allows canals to be easily dug and maintained, ensuring smooth water flow for irrigation purposes.
 
• The region is drained by numerous **perennial rivers**, such as the Ganga, Yamuna, Brahmaputra, and their tributaries. These rivers provide a consistent and reliable source of water throughout the year, essential for canal irrigation.
 
• The availability of **alluvial soil** in the northern plains further supports canal irrigation as this soil type retains water efficiently, making it suitable for agriculture. This facilitates the cultivation of water-intensive crops like rice, sugarcane, and wheat.
 
• The presence of a dense population in the northern plains increases the demand for irrigation to sustain agricultural activities, making canal irrigation a preferred choice for meeting the water needs of farmers.
 
• The historical development of extensive canal systems, such as the **Upper Ganga Canal**, has contributed to the region's agricultural productivity, making it one of the most fertile areas in India.

• The plains extend over an area of approximately **7 lakh square kilometers**, covering parts of Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and West Bengal.
 
• These plains are known for their **fertility** and are often referred to as the "Granary of India."
 
 
 
• **Advantages of Canal Irrigation:**
 
 
• Canal irrigation ensures **water availability even during dry seasons**, supporting year-round agriculture.
 
• It helps in controlling floods by diverting excess water into canals during periods of heavy rainfall.
 
• Canals often recharge the groundwater table, contributing to the sustainability of water resources.
 
 
 
• **Challenges of Canal Irrigation:**
 
 
• Canals require substantial **initial investment** for construction and maintenance, making them expensive.
 
• Waterlogging and soil salinity issues can arise in areas with poor drainage facilities.
 
• The equitable distribution of water can be a challenge, often leading to conflicts between upstream and downstream users.
 
 
 
• **Other Methods of Irrigation in India:**
 
 
• **Tube Wells:** Widely used in areas with abundant groundwater, particularly in Punjab, Haryana, and Uttar Pradesh.
 
• **Drip Irrigation:** A modern method used mainly for water-scarce regions, ensuring water efficiency.
 
• **Sprinkler Irrigation:** Used for areas with uneven terrain or sandy soils, commonly seen in Rajasthan and parts of Gujarat.
 
 
 
• **Perennial River Systems:**
 
 
• Perennial rivers like the Ganga and Brahmaputra are fed by **glaciers and monsoons**, ensuring a continuous supply of water.
 
• These rivers form a dense drainage network in the northern plains, making the region highly suitable for canal irrigation.

questions.question: Which of the following pollutants is/are primarily responsible for causing acid rain?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Acid rain** is primarily caused by the emission of **sulphur dioxide (SO₂)** and **nitrogen oxides (NOₓ)** into the atmosphere.
 
• These gases react with water vapor, oxygen, and other chemicals in the atmosphere to form **sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄)** and **nitric acid (HNO₃)**, which then mix with rainwater, making it acidic.
 
• **Sulphur dioxide** is mainly released from the burning of fossil fuels such as coal and oil in power plants and industrial facilities.
 
• **Nitrogen oxides** are emitted primarily from vehicle exhausts and industrial processes that involve combustion at high temperatures.
 
• This phenomenon leads to environmental damage, including the acidification of lakes and rivers, damage to forests, and deterioration of buildings and infrastructure. *Hence, the correct option is Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Formation of Acid Rain:**

 
 
• Acid rain is caused when **sulphur dioxide (SO₂)** and **nitrogen oxides (NOₓ)** combine with water vapor in the atmosphere to form acids.
 
• The chemical reactions involve the formation of **sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄)** and **nitric acid (HNO₃)**, which dissolve in rainwater.
 
• The pH of acid rain is usually less than **5.6**, making it harmful to natural and man-made environments.
 
 
 
• **Effects of Acid Rain:**
 
 
• Acid rain can cause the acidification of lakes, rivers, and streams, severely affecting aquatic life.
 
• It leads to the leaching of essential nutrients from the soil, adversely impacting plant growth and forest ecosystems.
 
• It accelerates the corrosion of buildings, monuments, and infrastructure, especially those made of limestone and marble.
 
• Acid rain can have indirect effects on human health by contaminating water sources and food chains.
 
 
 
• **Sources of Sulphur Dioxide and Nitrogen Oxides:**
 
 
• **Sulphur dioxide (SO₂):** The primary sources are coal-fired power plants, oil refineries, and industrial processes.
 
• **Nitrogen oxides (NOₓ):** These gases are mainly emitted by vehicles, industrial facilities, and power generation plants.
 
 
 
• **Prevention and Control of Acid Rain:**
 
 
• Reducing the use of fossil fuels by transitioning to renewable energy sources like solar and wind power.
 
• Implementing technologies such as **flue gas desulfurization** (FGD) to remove sulphur dioxide from exhaust emissions.
 
• Using catalytic converters in vehicles to minimize nitrogen oxide emissions.
 
• Promoting energy efficiency and enforcing stricter environmental regulations to limit industrial emissions.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• Acid rain was first identified as a serious environmental issue in the mid-20th century, particularly in industrialized regions.
 
• International agreements such as the **Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution (CLRTAP)** have been instrumental in reducing acid rain by controlling emissions of SO₂ and NOₓ.
 
• The **Clean Air Act** in the **United States** was amended in **1990** to establish programs to reduce acid rain.

questions.question: Which acid and its salts are widely used as food preservatives to prevent the growth of mould, yeast and fungi?

__
 
• **Sorbic acid** and its salts, such as potassium sorbate, are widely used as **food preservatives** to prevent the growth of **mould, yeast, and fungi**.

• It is effective in low concentrations and is commonly used in **processed foods, beverages, and bakery products** to maintain quality and safety.
 
• Sorbic acid has **antifungal properties** and inhibits microbial growth by interfering with the metabolic processes of fungi and yeast.
 
• Due to its **low toxicity** and safety for human consumption, sorbic acid is approved by food safety authorities worldwide, including the **US FDA** and the **European Food Safety Authority (EFSA)**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Perchloric Acid:**

 
 
• **Perchloric acid** is a strong mineral acid primarily used in industrial and laboratory applications.
 
• It is not used as a food preservative due to its corrosive and highly reactive properties.
 
• Applications include **oxidation reactions** and the preparation of perchlorate salts.
 
 
 
• **Boric Acid:**
 
 
• **Boric acid** is a weak acid with applications in antiseptics, insecticides, and industrial products.
 
• It is not a primary food preservative due to concerns about its **toxicity** when ingested in large amounts.
 
• Boric acid is used in small amounts as a pH buffer in some industrial food preparation processes.
 
 
 
• **Malic Acid:**
 
 
• **Malic acid** is a naturally occurring organic acid found in fruits such as apples and cherries.
 
• It is primarily used in the food and beverage industry as a **flavor enhancer** and acidulant.
 
• While it contributes to the tangy taste of foods, it does not have **antimicrobial properties** like sorbic acid.
 
 
 
• **Sorbic Acid:**
 
 
• Sorbic acid is widely used in foods such as **cheese, wine, dried fruits, and soft drinks**.
 
• Potassium sorbate, a salt of sorbic acid, is highly soluble and often preferred for use in liquid products.
 
• It is effective in **acidic environments**, making it suitable for preserving acidic foods like fruit juices.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Sorbic Acid:**
 
 
• Used in **pharmaceuticals** to prevent microbial contamination of medicines.
 
• Commonly used in **cosmetics** to extend the shelf life of products by preventing microbial growth.
 
• Acts as an antifungal agent in food packaging materials.

questions.question: Which organelle is responsible for photosynthesis in plants?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Chloroplast**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Chloroplasts** are the organelles responsible for **photosynthesis** in plants, enabling them to convert sunlight into chemical energy stored as glucose.
 
• They contain the pigment **chlorophyll**, which absorbs light energy primarily from the **blue and red wavelengths** of sunlight, facilitating the photosynthetic process.
 
• Photosynthesis occurs in two main phases: the **light-dependent reactions** (in the thylakoid membranes) and the **Calvin cycle** (in the stroma).
 
• The chloroplast structure includes the **thylakoid membranes**, stroma, and grana, which are essential for trapping light energy and synthesizing sugars.
 
• Chloroplasts are **unique to plants and algae**, and their ability to perform photosynthesis is critical for the survival of most life forms on Earth.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mitochondria:**

 
 
• Known as the **powerhouse of the cell**, mitochondria are responsible for generating **ATP** (adenosine triphosphate) through cellular respiration.
 
• They do not participate in photosynthesis but play a crucial role in energy production within plant and animal cells.
 
• Mitochondria have a double membrane structure and their own DNA, enabling them to replicate independently of the cell.

questions.question: Which of the following options correctly describes the scope of judicial review under the Constitution of India?

options.text: Only the Supreme Court can declare laws unconstitutional.
Judicial review is explicitly mentioned in the Constitution (Article 13).
Both, Supreme Court and High Courts can strike down unconstitutional laws.
Courts can review any law only after approval by the Parliament

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both, Supreme Court and High Courts can strike down unconstitutional laws.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Judicial Review** is the power of the judiciary to review and determine the constitutionality of legislative and executive actions. It is a vital component of India's democracy.
 
• Both the **Supreme Court** and the **High Courts** in India have the authority to perform judicial review under Articles **32** and **226** of the Constitution, respectively. *Hence, this statement is correct.*
 
• **Article 13** explicitly mentions that laws inconsistent with or in derogation of the Fundamental Rights shall be void. This forms the foundation of judicial review in India. *Hence, this statement is correct.*
 
• The judiciary does not need prior approval from the Parliament to review laws. It can independently assess laws based on petitions or suo moto actions. *Thus, this statement is incorrect.*
 
• The Supreme Court is the final interpreter of the Constitution, while High Courts exercise judicial review for matters within their territorial jurisdiction.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Judicial Review in India:**

 
 
• Judicial review is a part of the basic structure of the Constitution as established by the **Keshavananda Bharati Case (1973).**
 
• It ensures that the legislative and executive actions remain within the limits set by the Constitution.
 
• This mechanism protects the Fundamental Rights of citizens and maintains the supremacy of the Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Role of the Supreme Court:**
 
 
• The Supreme Court has original jurisdiction under **Article 32** to enforce Fundamental Rights and strike down unconstitutional laws.
 
• It has appellate jurisdiction to review decisions of lower courts and tribunals.
 
• Judicial review by the Supreme Court applies to the entire country.
 
 
 
• **Role of High Courts:**
 
 
• High Courts exercise judicial review under **Article 226**, which empowers them to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights and other legal rights.
 
• Judicial review by High Courts is limited to their territorial jurisdiction.
 
 
 
• **Important Cases related to Judicial Review:**
 
 
• **Marbury v. Madison (1803):** This US case established the concept of judicial review, which influenced its adoption in India.
 
• **A. K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950):** This case was one of the earliest instances of judicial review in India.
 
• **Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978):** This case expanded the scope of judicial review to include due process in administrative actions.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Constitutional Provisions:**

 
 
• **Article 13:** Declares laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights void, forming the backbone of judicial review.
 
• **Article 32:** Empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
 
• **Article 226:** Grants High Courts the power to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights and other legal rights.
 
 
 
• **Limitations of Judicial Review:**
 
 
• Judicial review cannot extend to political questions or policy decisions unless they violate the Constitution.
 
• It does not grant the judiciary legislative or executive powers; it only ensures constitutional compliance.
 
 
 
• **Significance:**
 
 
• Judicial review acts as a check on arbitrary legislative and executive actions.
 
• It upholds the principle of separation of powers and ensures the rule of law in a democracy.

questions.question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution states that a person who had voluntarily acquired the citizenship of a foreign State shall NOT be considered a citizen of India at the commencement of the Constitution under Articles 5, 6, or 8?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 9**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 9** of the **Indian Constitution** states that a person who has voluntarily acquired the citizenship of any foreign country shall not be considered a citizen of India at the commencement of the Constitution.
 
• This provision ensures that individuals who have deliberately chosen to acquire foreign citizenship are excluded from Indian citizenship, despite Articles 5, 6, or 8.
 
• Articles 5, 6, and 8 of the Constitution deal with citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution. However, Article 9 specifically overrides these provisions for individuals who have voluntarily acquired foreign citizenship.
 
• Article 9 establishes the principle of exclusivity in citizenship, disallowing dual citizenship under the Indian legal framework.
 
• The provision reflects the framers' intention to maintain a single allegiance to India, ensuring that citizenship is not divided between India and a foreign state.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 5:**

 
 
• Article 5 defines the citizenship of people who were domiciled in India at the commencement of the Constitution (January 26, 1950).
 
• It states that anyone born in the territory of India, or whose parents were born in India, or who has been an ordinary resident for five years immediately preceding the commencement of the Constitution, is deemed a citizen of India.
 
 
 
• **Article 6:**
 
 
• Article 6 addresses the rights of certain persons who migrated to India from Pakistan before July 19, 1948, granting them Indian citizenship under specific conditions.
 
 
 
• **Article 8:**
 
 
• Article 8 provides citizenship rights to individuals of Indian origin residing outside India at the commencement of the Constitution, provided their father or grandfather was born in India.
 
• Such individuals must register with an Indian diplomatic or consular representative to be recognized as Indian citizens.
 
 
 
• **Citizenship Act, 1955:**
 
 
• The **Citizenship Act, 1955**, governs the acquisition, termination, and supplementary provisions of Indian citizenship.
 
• It lays down five modes of acquiring Indian citizenship: by birth, descent, registration, naturalization, and incorporation of territory.
 
 
 
• **Concept of Single Citizenship:**
 
 
• The Indian Constitution provides for **single citizenship**, meaning that all Indians, regardless of the state or territory they belong to, are citizens of India.
 
• This is in contrast to countries like the United States, which follow a dual citizenship model (federal and state citizenship).

• In the **K. Umadevi v. Government of Tamil Nadu case (2022)**, the **Supreme Court of India** granted maternity benefits for the third child under the **Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017**. The decision emphasized that these benefits are a **constitutional right**.

• By extending maternity benefits to the third child, the Court underlined the importance of ensuring a dignified life for mothers and children, aligning with the broader interpretation of the **Right to Life** under Article 21.

questions.question: Colonial policies led to the commercialisation of agriculture. Which of the following crops was encouraged for export during British rule?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The colonial policies during British rule in India led to the **commercialisation of agriculture**, where farmers were forced to focus on producing cash crops for export rather than food crops for domestic consumption.
 
• **Indigo**, a plant used for producing blue dye, was one of the most significant crops encouraged for export by the British due to its high demand in the European textile industry. *Hence, this is the correct option.*
 
• The British established indigo plantations and compelled Indian farmers to grow indigo under exploitative systems like the **nij system** and the **ryoti system**.
 
• Farmers were often paid very low prices for indigo, leading to significant economic hardship and causing revolts such as the **Indigo Rebellion of 1859–1860** in Bengal.
 
• Other crops encouraged by the British for export included **cotton, tea, and opium**, but indigo played a particularly pivotal role in the colonial economy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Commercialisation of Agriculture:**

 
 
• The British introduced commercialisation of agriculture in India to serve the needs of the **Industrial Revolution in Britain**.
 
• Farmers were forced to cultivate cash crops such as **indigo, cotton, and opium**, which were exported to Europe.
 
• This shift disrupted traditional agricultural practices, leading to food shortages, famines, and poverty among Indian peasants.
 
 
 
• **Indigo Cultivation in India:**
 
 
• Indigo dye was in high demand in Europe during the 18th and 19th centuries, especially in the **textile industry**.
 
• The British imposed the **ryoti system**, under which farmers were forced to grow indigo on their land and sell it at extremely low prices to British planters.
 
• The exploitation of Indian farmers led to the **Indigo Rebellion** in Bengal, where peasants protested against the oppressive practices of British indigo planters.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Indigo Cultivation:**
 
 
• Indigo cultivation depleted soil fertility, leaving land unsuitable for growing food crops, causing severe economic distress.
 
• The profits from indigo exports benefited the British economy, while Indian farmers suffered **debt and poverty**.
 
• The **Indigo Commission of 1860** was set up to address the grievances of indigo farmers, but its impact was limited.
 
 
 
• **Comparison of Other Crops:**
 
 
• **Maize:** A staple food crop, not primarily grown for export during British rule.
 
• **Barley:** Another food crop with limited export significance under colonial policies.
 
• **Pulses:** Essential for domestic consumption, not encouraged for export by the British.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Indigo Rebellion:**

 
 
• The Indigo Rebellion of 1859-60 was a significant peasant uprising in Bengal against the exploitative practices of British indigo planters.
 
• It highlighted the plight of farmers under colonial policies and inspired later movements for agricultural reforms.
 
 
 
• **Economic Exploitation:**
 
 
• The British policies of forced cultivation of cash crops like indigo were part of a broader system of economic exploitation in colonial India.
 
• These policies contributed to widespread poverty and food insecurity among Indian farmers.

• **Evolution of Tamasha:**

 
 
• Initially performed in village fairs and festivals, Tamasha became an organized theatre form with professional troupes emerging during the **18th century.**
 
• Modern Tamasha performances have adapted to urban audiences, incorporating **new themes** while retaining traditional elements.
 
 
 
• **Influence on Other Art Forms:**
 
 
• Tamasha has influenced Marathi cinema and music, with several filmmakers integrating its themes and styles into their works.
 
• The folk art form continues to inspire contemporary artists, preserving the cultural legacy of Maharashtra.

questions.question: PM Modi’s review of NTEP in May 2025 urged volunteers called _____________ to adopt AI tools for patient follow‑up.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Nikshay Mitras**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Nikshay Mitras** is a volunteer initiative under the **Pradhan Mantri TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan** launched to combat **Tuberculosis (TB)** in India.
 
• Under the **Nikshay Mitra** program, volunteers adopt TB patients and assist them with nutritional support, treatment adherence, and regular follow-ups.
 
• During the review of **National Tuberculosis Elimination Program (NTEP)** in **May 2025**, **PM Narendra Modi** emphasized the use of **Artificial Intelligence (AI)** tools to enhance patient follow-up and monitoring.
 
• The **National Tuberculosis Elimination Program (NTEP)** aims to eliminate TB by **2025**, five years ahead of the global target set by the World Health Organization (WHO).
 
• Volunteers, termed **Nikshay Mitras**, play a crucial role in achieving the target by ensuring personalized care and reducing the burden of TB patients.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **National Tuberculosis Elimination Program (NTEP):**

 
 
• NTEP was previously known as the Revised National Tuberculosis Control Program (**RNTCP**).
 
• It focuses on active case finding, treatment adherence, and preventive measures to eliminate TB by **2025**.
 
• The program aligns with the **Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)** and aims to reduce TB incidence and mortality significantly.
 
• India is the highest TB burden country globally, accounting for nearly **26%** of the global TB cases.
 
• NTEP incorporates advanced technologies such as **AI tools** for monitoring and addressing patient needs.
 
 
 
• **Pradhan Mantri TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan:**
 
 
• Launched on **September 9, 2022**, this initiative seeks community participation in TB elimination efforts.
 
• **Nikshay Mitras** adopt TB patients and provide nutritional and psychological support.
 
• Volunteers register through the **Nikshay 2.0 portal**, a digital platform for TB patient management.
 
• Support packages include **monthly food baskets** and assistance in accessing healthcare facilities.
 
 
 
• **Role of Artificial Intelligence in TB Management:**
 
 
• **AI** tools are used for predictive analytics to identify high-risk patients and ensure targeted interventions.
 
• AI helps in improving diagnostic accuracy, especially in resource-constrained areas.
 
• Patient follow-ups and medication adherence are enhanced through AI-based monitoring systems.
 
• The integration of AI in NTEP aligns with India's commitment to using technology for public health improvement.
 
 
 
• **Global TB Elimination Efforts:**
 
 
• The **World Health Organization (WHO)** aims to eliminate TB globally by **2030** under its **End TB Strategy**.
 
• India's goal of eliminating TB by **2025** demonstrates a proactive approach and commitment to public health.
 
• International collaboration and funding are crucial for achieving the set targets.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Facts about TB:**

 
 
• **Tuberculosis** is a bacterial infection caused by **Mycobacterium tuberculosis**, primarily affecting the lungs.
 
• It spreads through airborne transmission when an infected person coughs or sneezes.
 
• India accounts for the highest number of TB cases globally, making it a public health priority.
 
• The disease is preventable and curable with early diagnosis and complete treatment adherence.
 
 
 
• **Nikshay Portal:**
 
 
• The **Nikshay Portal** is a digital tool used for TB patient registration, monitoring, and support.
 
• It facilitates real-time tracking of patient outcomes and treatment adherence.
 
• The portal plays a vital role in integrating technology with healthcare delivery systems.
